function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a complete “starter kit” that you can drop into the **nodejs‑welcome** repository.  
It contains:

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a lightweight Node.js image for the app |
| `k8s.yaml` | Deployment + Service for Kubernetes |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | GitHub Actions workflow that builds the image and runs tests on every push to `main` |

> **NOTE** – The Docker image is built locally and pushed to a registry that you configure via GitHub Secrets (`DOCKER_USERNAME`, `DOCKER_PASSWORD`).  
> If you prefer another registry (GitHub Container Registry, ECR, GCR, …) just change the `docker login` step accordingly.

---

## 1. Dockerfile

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# Base image – Alpine gives a small footprint
FROM node:18-alpine

# Working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install production dependencies only
RUN npm install --production

# Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port your app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Default command
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> *If your app listens on a different port, change `EXPOSE 3000` and the `containerPort` in the Kubernetes manifest accordingly.*

---

## 2. Kubernetes YAML (`k8s.yaml`)

```yaml
# k8s.yaml
# ------------------------------------
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: nodejs-welcome:latest   # will be overridden by image tag in CI
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000

---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80          # external port
    targetPort: 3000  # container port
```

> *If you want a LoadBalancer or NodePort, change `type` under `Service`.*

---

## 3. GitHub Actions Workflow (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`)

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3

      # Set up Node.js
      - name: Set up Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v3
        with:
          node-version: '18'

      # Install dependencies
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      # Run tests (adjust if your test script is named differently)
      - name: Run tests
        run: npm test

      # Build Docker image
      - name: Build Docker image
        run: |
          docker build -t nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} .

      # Log in to Docker registry (replace with your registry if needed)
      - name: Docker login
        uses: docker/login-action@v2
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_PASSWORD }}

      # Push image to registry
      - name: Push Docker image
        run: |
          docker push nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
```

> **Secrets required**  
> * `DOCKER_USERNAME` – your Docker registry username  
> * `DOCKER_PASSWORD` – your Docker registry password or token  

> If you’re using GitHub Container Registry, replace the login step with:
> ```yaml
> - uses: docker/login-action@v2
>   with:
>     registry: ghcr.io
>     username: ${{ github.actor }}
>     password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
> ```

---

## 4. Add, Commit & Push

```bash
# From the root of the repository
git add Dockerfile k8s.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically run on the next commit to `main`.  
> The Docker image will be tagged with the commit SHA (`nodejs-welcome:<sha>`) and pushed to the registry you configured.

---

### Quick Recap

1. **Clone** the repo locally (you already have it).  
2. **Create** the three files above.  
3. **Commit** and **push**.  
4. **Verify** that the Actions tab shows a successful run and that the image appears in your registry.

That’s it! Your Node.js app now has a Docker image, Kubernetes deployment, and continuous integration pipeline—all ready to go. Happy coding!
